newsitem.title: UK: Mother's diet linked to baby's bowel problems.
newsitem.headline: Mother's diet linked to baby's bowel problems.

text.p: Women who eat a low-fibre diet while pregnant may give birth to babies more prone to bowel disease, British researchers said on Tuesday.
Dr Linda Weiss and colleagues at the University of Stirling said that rats fed a low-fibre diet while pregnant gave birth to babies prone to diverticulosis, a common bowel disorder.

They took two groups of rats and fed one a high-fibre diet, which would be high in vegetable content, and another a low- fibre diet before mating. They then fed their babies either a high or low fibre diet.
Those whose mothers had been fed a low-fibre diet were twice as likely to develop diverticulosis, whether they got fibre in their diets or not, Weiss wrote in the journal Gut.
She said her findings could apply to people.
Low-fibre diets dominated by such foods as meat and dairy products are linked with diverticulosis in adults. The condition occurs when diverticula, or little cavities, form in the colon.
Bits of faecal matter pile up in them and become painfully infected.

Weiss said it was not clear what was happening with the rats but thought it could have something to do with microbes transmitted in mother's milk. The make-up of bacteria in the gut is important to digestion.
She said the findings added to evidence that diet during pregnancy and breast-feeding could have a major influence on the development of gastrointestinal disease in later life.
